extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society, 17th-century natural philosophers, anatomists and experimental physicians
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of 17th-century experimental reports and observational accounts describing anatomical procedures (nerve sectioning), transfusion and vein-injection techniques, microscopic anatomy, field observations (tides, wells, whale-fishing), and a computational method for the Julian period. Contains procedural steps, experimental precautions, and interpretive remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for producing wind-broken respiration by severing diaphragmatic nerves
rubrics_metrics.description: Step-by-step surgical method to divide the nerves of the diaphragm in a dog to reproduce wind-broken (paradoxical) respiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original guidance: "pierce the side of the animal between the 6th and 7th rib in the middle of the thorax... put in a director or a small quill... thrust it in about an inch, directing the end of it toward the sternum... then cut upon it about an inch on the intercostal muscles;... put in your finger, and with your nail separate the nerve... lay hold of the nerve and pull it to the orifice of the breast, and cut it off, and sew the hole up very close. Do the same on the other side, and presently let the dog loose..." Precaution: "let him first take notice how the nerves of the diaphragm pass along on each side of the pericardium in a dead animal, before the trial be attempted in a living one." Also advises making the incision shallow to avoid touching the lungs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation: Inversion of abdominal movement in wind-broken animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical observation of how abdominal movement is reversed after diaphragmatic nerve division: on inspiration the belly is drawn in, and on expiration the belly relaxes and swells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as the first 'obvious remark' on the experiment: useful diagnostic/observational criterion to recognise diaphragmatic nerve dysfunction in animals (and by analogy in horses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: lungs depend on thorax expansion by muscles and diaphragm
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiological inference that lungs do not move of themselves but depend on expansion of the thorax by intercostal muscles and the diaphragm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the experiment: 'all inspiration being made by the dilatation of the thorax... caused partly by the intercostal muscles... and partly... the diaphragm by its contraction.' Used to infer how each component compensates when the other is disabled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis: wind-broken condition may result from rupture/relaxation of diaphragmatic nerves
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference that wind-broken breathing in horses (and similar conditions) is 'more than probable' to arise from relaxation or rupture of the nerves of the diaphragm (e.g., caused by straining).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to connect experimental nerve sectioning in dogs to naturally occurring disease in horses; suggests a causal diagnostic criterion for veterinary medicine in these cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgical precautions to avoid lung injury during thoracic nerve section
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific procedural measure: make the incision on the intercostal muscles over a director/quill to be secured from touching the lungs with the point or edge of the knife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit anti-pattern: do not penetrate lung tissue; use director/quill as shield and cut only about an inch on the intercostal muscles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical–anatomical correlation for pleural/mediastinal effusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Postmortem description and correlation: repeated pulmonary and febrile complaints, dyspnoea and inability to lie on left side correspond to a large pleural bag with milky/thick fluid occupying much of the chest cavity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: 'bag ran along from the left shoulder to the extremity of the right side of the midriff... contained about three pints' and lung lobes wasted where bag occupied space. Use of external clinical signs to suspect pleural accumulation; on dissection examine pleura and mediastinum for 'bag' and thick milky fluid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and report anatomical variations (vas praeparans origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Note and report observed anatomical deviations, e.g. 'the right vas praeparans sprang clearly from the right emulgent; whereas ordinarily the vas praeparans arises on the right side out of the aorta...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages careful documentation of departures from typical anatomy as part of anatomical observation. No specific corrective action, but explicit value placed on noting variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental observation: effects of adding various liquids to warm blood
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical findings about mixing warm blood with different liquids: adding aqua fortis, oil of vitriol, or spirit of salt causes blood to lose pure colour and coagulate; mixing with 'urinous spirit' (volatile salts, spirit of sal ammoniac) keeps blood fluid, makes it more florid, and preserves it from putrefaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a procedural/experimental note about reagents' effects on warm blood and as support for later injections/transfusion experiments. Suggests further trials with other liquors (spirit of wine, oil of tartar, oil of turpentine) and observations on colour of upper part of blood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for transfusion of animal blood into a human vein (procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stepwise account of a human transfusion from a sheep: prepare carotid artery in sheep, insert a silver pipe into quills to let blood run to a porringer to measure flow; prepare human vein, make incision, let 6–7 ounces bleed, plant silver pipe into vein, use quills between pipes to convey arterial blood from sheep into man's vein; allow blood to run about two minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes on practicalities: choose pipe size appropriate to vein (they used a smaller pipe when human vein seemed too small), monitor pulse in the vein beyond the pipe as indication of flow, and be alert to coagulation in pipes. Suggests repeating experiments with more exact weighing of donor before and after to quantify blood loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations on pipe length, temperature and coagulation in transfusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational guidance that long pipes can cool blood (patient may not feel blood as hot) and that blood is apt to coagulate in pipes upon the least stop, especially when pipes are long (e.g., three quills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: minimize pipe length to preserve heat and reduce coagulation risk; avoid stops/obstructions in pipes; design pipes to be as short and wide as feasible for freer flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement practice recommendation for transfusion quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation to weigh the emitting (donor) animal before and after the operation to obtain a more just account of the quantity of blood lost/transfused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as an improvement to be applied in subsequent repeats to obtain more accurate quantitative data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method and observed effects of injecting medicated (laxative) liquors into veins
rubrics_metrics.description: Protocol: inject ~two drams of a laxative medicine by a syphon into the median vein of the right arm; observed effects: local pain and swelling at injection site, vomiting soon after, catharsis (multiple stools), and in one case disappearance of exostoses/pustular symptoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes and cautions: swelling of arm valves required gentle compression to move swelling toward shoulder; repeated vomiting was a common immediate effect; outcome variability (one subject died after taking cold and careless diet). Use of laxatives to produce conspicuous effects when changing medicines seems recommended for early trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field procedure for whale-hunting (practical guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of local practices for killing whales at Bermuda: strike in shoal water rather than deep water; boats manned with six oars; row up gently and the harpooner strikes the whale 'about or before the fins' rather than toward the tail; harping irons made of excellent metal and attached to flexible rope and staff which comes out of socket when struck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational tips: avoid striking deep-water whales (plunging dangerous); use well-made harping irons that bend not break; harpoon near fins; use small boats capable of forward/backward rowing; strike in shoal water and haul in when whale quiet; account of local differences (smaller, more lively whales than Greenland ones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation method for the Julian period (de Billy's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithm to find the number of the Julian period: multiply solar cycle, lunar cycle, and indiction remainders by fixed multipliers (4845, 4200, 6916 respectively), sum the products, divide the sum by 7980 (the Julian period) and take the remainder as the required Julian-year number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition and derivation of multipliers: each multiplier is divisible by all other divisors leaving remainder 0 but leaves remainder 1 when divided by its own divisor; the divisors (28, 19, 15) are pairwise primitive. Example provided with numbers and a demonstration of the arithmetic justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording and reporting of experimental side-effects and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice of reporting both positive outcomes and adverse/ambiguous results: examples include patients vomiting after vein injections, donor animal's blood potentially cooling in pipes, and the need to repeat with better quantification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly document adverse reactions and procedural limitations, suggest methodological refinements (weighing donor, adjusting pipe shape/length) and caution against overclaiming benefits without repeatable measures.
